source.title: Are wider nets better given the same number of parameters?
source.authors: A. Golubeva; Behnam Neyshabur; Guy Gur-Ari

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. No evident truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly sweeps network width while holding parameter count fixed and measures test accuracy, with some training-accuracy results. This is a different intervention from widening beyond the interpolation threshold in V2, but tests how width relates to held-out performance.
record.gate_note: Own results include test-accuracy sweeps for sparse wide models, bottleneck methods, and kernel-distance measurements. Cited prior findings are not extracted. Figure-only ResNet-18 curves are not assigned reconstructed point values; numeric table and text-described results are recorded.
record.test_reason: Section 2.3 explicitly reports improved test performance from widening even for ResNet-18 models that fit the training set. This tests V2 in a new setting: convolutional networks widened through static sparsity at fixed weight count, with weight decay. Other width improvements do not by themselves establish improvement beyond the width needed to fit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. Static random sparsity permits widening at fixed weight count and improves image-classification accuracy. Width accounts for most gains while sparse models retain high training accuracy. The GP-kernel experiment supports a proposed explanation through correlation, rather than establishing it causally.
record.recipe_differences: The main intervention is width increase at fixed parameter count using randomly chosen static sparsity, evaluated with test accuracy; V2 concerns width beyond the zero-training-error threshold without explicit regularization. The study also evaluates bottlenecks. Weight decay is used in the ResNet-18 experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with activation (ReLU versus linear), width, baseline model size, dataset, and sparsity distribution. At extreme sparsity, training accuracy deteriorates; performance peaks at a dataset- and model-dependent widening factor.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-weight sparse widening improves MNIST accuracy from approximately 90% to 96.3% with ReLU and 92.7% with linear activations, without establishing training-set interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse widening at fixed weight count can improve held-out accuracy in narrow MLPs.

fits_no_version.finding: ImageNet sparse ResNet-18 accuracy increases from 68.03% at width 64 to 70.66% at width 181, then reaches 70.53% at width 256.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed-weight sparse widening can improve image-classification accuracy up to a workload-dependent width, including when training accuracy remains below 100%.

fits_no_version.finding: For small ResNet-18 models at low connectivity, distributing sparsity across all tensor dimensions outperforms removing whole spatial kernels, with gaps up to 3 percentage points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The distribution of static sparsity affects held-out accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The sparse MLP's best trained performance occurs at a width similar to the minimum initialization GP-kernel distance from the infinite-width dense kernel.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization GP-kernel distance tracks performance in the studied sparse MLP.

record.problems: ImageNet runs were not repeated; only two datapoints had seed variance checked. Most ResNet-18 curve values are presented in figures rather than stated numerically. Width improvements depend on the model reaching high training accuracy and on the selected sparsity distribution.
record.rows_left_out: No reported findings required omission under the 60-row limit. Values from Figures 1, 6, 7, and 9 were not transcribed where the text gives no exact point values; relevant figure-only outcomes and descriptions are recorded in R4–R6 and R8.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.

The original dense, one-hidden-layer ReLU recipe without explicit regularization; an identified fitting threshold and test-error trajectory beyond it for the MNIST MLPs; training to convergence for the ResNet experiments.
Convolutional versus fully connected performance and the contribution of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and sensitivity to tuning.
Batch-size effects and adaptations that recover held-out performance.
Dropout effects and interactions with data size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization gaps, and rankings against alternative measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Extreme-sparsity failures that also destroy training fit do not challenge V2's post-fit claim. Linear-network results and comparisons against dense models of the same width likewise do not establish limitations of that claim. No numerical values were reconstructed from figure curves.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label generalization comparison.

Does not test widening past the width needed for zero training error under the V2 recipe; the central sweeps hold parameter count fixed using static sparsity, and report test accuracy and selected training-accuracy descriptions rather than a direct interpolation-threshold sweep.
No comparison of convolutional networks with fully connected networks trained from scratch.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or training-to-test gap ranking comparison.

rows.subject: MLP with 1 hidden layer, ReLU activations
rows.operation_detail: Swept width and layer connectivity with total weights fixed at 3970; compared test accuracy.
rows.note: Authors state the baseline accuracy is approximately 90%; the reported maximum is reached by two width/connectivity settings.
rows.check: The numerical improvement is correctly recorded, but training-set fit is not established. It cannot demonstrate V2's improvement beyond the fitting threshold.

rows.subject: MLP with 1 hidden layer, linear activations
rows.operation_detail: Swept width and layer connectivity with total weights fixed at 3970; compared test accuracy.
rows.note: Widening yields a modest maximum increase over the approximately 90% baseline.
rows.check: This is a linear network, and training-set fit is not established. The smaller accuracy gain is not evidence limiting V2's ReLU-network claim.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.size_stated: ImageNet baseline width 64; 11.7 million weights; sparse variants keep the same weight count
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; SGD with momentum=0.9; 150 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Compared dense and static-random-sparse width variants while holding sparse-model weight count fixed.

conditions.value: random static mask; layerwise distribution proportional to layer size

rows.value: 69.56 at width 90 sparse (11.7 million weights); 70.02 at width 128 sparse (11.7 million weights); 70.66 at width 181 sparse (11.7 million weights); 70.53 at width 256 sparse (11.7 million weights)
rows.uncertainty: not stated for these runs; ImageNet experiments were not repeated, and two checked datapoints had variance smaller than 0.1% across random seeds
rows.note: Text says gains are comparable to widening dense models only up to a certain width; dense comparison values are 69.11 (width 90), 70.22 (128), 70.91 (181), and 71.89 (256).
rows.check: Table 1 values are correct, but these ImageNet models do not fit the training set; Figure 13 shows training accuracy well below 100%. Neither the gain nor its eventual decline tests widening beyond the fitting threshold.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; SGD with momentum=0.9; 300 epochs on non-ImageNet datasets
rows.operation_detail: Swept width at fixed parameter count with static random sparsity, measuring test accuracy.

conditions.value: random static mask; weights removed proportionally to layer size

rows.uncertainty: error bars shown in Appendix Figure 11; values not stated in text
rows.note: Authors state test performance improves with width at fixed parameter count up to a certain widening factor, and that the effect is present even for models that fit the training set. The curves are not transcribed into point estimates.
rows.check: Restrict the V2 link to models that fit the training set, as explicitly described in Section 2.3. Split datasets and model sizes where the figures permit; the aggregate row also includes underfitting models outside that condition. The sparsity allocation is a staged removal procedure described in Appendix D, rather than uniform proportional removal.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.3; Figure 6 and caption; Appendix A; Appendix E, Figures 11–14.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; SGD with momentum=0.9; 300 epochs on non-ImageNet datasets
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-accuracy behavior across width and connectivity in the fixed-parameter-count sparse sweeps.
rows.value: figure only; larger models attain 100% training accuracy, while smaller models' training accuracy rises and then deteriorates as connectivity decreases further
rows.note: Training accuracy helps locate where sparse connectivity begins to impair optimization; exact curve values are not stated.
rows.check: Training accuracy supplies the fitting condition for R4 but does not itself measure the held-out improvement named by V2. Keep as contextual evidence rather than an independent generalization result.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared two convolutional-layer sparsity distributions in sparse wide models.

conditions.value: remove weights across all tensor dimensions versus input/output dimensions only

rows.value: figure only; all-dimension removal performs better for smaller models, with a gap up to 3% on CIFAR datasets
rows.note: A condition on how sparsity is distributed changes the outcome; the text reports up to a 3% test-accuracy gap for the smaller models and small connectivity.
rows.check: This compares sparsity distributions, not post-fit widening. The reported gap up to 3 percentage points concerns base widths 8 and 12 on both CIFAR datasets; Figure 9 displays CIFAR-100 and also includes width 18.

rows.subject: MLP with 1 hidden layer, no biases, ReLU activation
rows.size_stated: dense width varied; sparse models have 6,352 weights, equal to dense width 8
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; vanilla SGD; 300 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Swept width at fixed sparse parameter count and measured test accuracy and initialization kernel distance.

conditions.value: subset of 2048 MNIST training samples; full MNIST test set

rows.uncertainty: averages over 10 random seeds; no numerical uncertainty stated
rows.note: Text says optimal trained performance and minimal initialization kernel distance occur at a similar width; precise test-accuracy values by width are figure-only.
rows.check: The width-dependent test performance is relevant background, but no training-accuracy result establishes which models fit the 2048 training examples. It therefore cannot establish the post-fit behavior specified by V2.

rows.subject: MLP with 1 hidden layer, no biases, ReLU activation
rows.size_stated: dense width varied; sparse models have 6,352 weights, equal to dense width 8
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean squared distance between the sparse model Gaussian Process kernel and the infinite-width dense kernel.

conditions.value: subset of 2048 MNIST training samples; full MNIST test set

rows.value: figure only; text reports the empirical and theoretical distances agree well when dp >> 1 and minimum distance occurs at a width similar to the optimal trained performance
rows.note: This measures kernel distance and its association with performance, not the generalization gap named by V7.
rows.check: Kernel distance is neither post-fit test-error improvement nor magnitude-aware sharpness. Its association with test performance fits no supplied version.

relationships.condition: ResNet-18 models that fit the training set, widened using static random sparsity at fixed weight count
relationships.reason: Section 2.3 explicitly states that the test-performance benefit persists for models fitting the training set; R4 records this qualitative result, with R5 supplying training-fit context.
relationships.display_finding: Widening at a fixed number of weights improved test performance among configurations that fit the training data, although extreme sparsity reduced training accuracy.
